lessons.title: What Drives the Cost of Protection: Time, Volatility, and India VIX

children.text: Home insurance in Mumbai does not get cheaper when the monsoon arrives. Options insurance works the same way, only faster and more brutally. In March 2020, with India VIX above 80, a put on the Nifty cost several times what the same protection had cost a few months earlier. Investors who decided to hedge after the crash had started paid peak prices for cover against a fall that had largely already happened. This lesson explains what sets the price of a put, why volatility is the dial that swings it most, and how to read India VIX before you buy.

body.text: Protection is priced by fear. When the market is calm, cover is cheap because nobody wants it. When the market is panicking, cover is expensive because everybody does. Hedgers who decide in calm markets pay a fraction of what hedgers who decide in a panic pay.

children.text: The Six Things That Set a Put's Price
You have already met two of these in earlier lessons. The strike is your deductible and the time to expiry is your policy term. The rest complete the picture.

children.text: Implied Volatility: The Market's Fear Gauge Inside Every Premium

markDefs.definition: The level of future volatility that the market is pricing into an option's premium, expressed as an annualised percentage. Higher implied volatility means more expensive options.

children.text: Every other input to a put's price is visible: the Nifty level, the strike, the days to expiry, the interest rate. The one thing nobody knows is how much the Nifty will move before expiry. The premium the market is willing to pay tells you how much movement it expects. Work backwards from that premium and you get
, or IV. When traders are nervous, they bid up puts, IV rises, and every hedger pays more for exactly the same strike and term.

body.caption: The same three-month Nifty 24,000 put at different implied volatility levels, Nifty at 25,000, one lot of 65 (illustrative model prices)

body.title: Cost of three months of cover (24,000 put) as implied volatility rises

body.text: Look at the bottom of that table. At 12% IV, three months of cover costs about half a percent. At 30%, the identical put costs 3.5%, close to a year's worth of calm-market hedging for a single quarter. The ₹250 premium used in earlier lessons corresponds to IV of roughly 15% to 16%, which is a fairly ordinary, calm market. Out-of-the-money puts usually also trade at a somewhat higher IV than at-the-money options, which is why real premiums sit a little above a flat-volatility model.

children.text: India VIX: Reading the Fear Gauge

You do not have to back out implied volatility yourself. NSE publishes India VIX, computed from the prices of near-month and next-month Nifty options. It is the market's expectation of Nifty volatility over the next 30 days, as an annualised percentage. A rising India VIX means puts are getting more expensive across the board. A falling India VIX means cover is getting cheaper.

body.label: India VIX is annualised
body.value: A VIX of 16 does not mean a 16% move this month
body.context: To convert it to an expected one-month move, divide by the square root of 12, roughly 3.46. A VIX of 16 implies a typical monthly move of about 4.6%.

body.caption: A rough one standard deviation range: the Nifty stays within this move in about two out of three months, if the market's expectation is right.

body.title: Translate the VIX
body.prompt: India VIX is at 20. Using the rule of thumb above, what is the market's expected one-month move in the Nifty, in percent? (One decimal place.)
body.explanation: 20 ÷ √12 = 20 ÷ 3.464 ≈ 5.77%, or about 5.8%. With the Nifty at 25,000, that is a typical monthly range of roughly ±1,440 points.

events.title: Global financial crisis
events.description: India VIX surged to its highest levels on record, around 85 to 90, as the Nifty collapsed about 60% from its January peak.

events.title: COVID crash
events.description: India VIX closed above 80 near the market bottom. Put premiums were several times their levels from a few months earlier.

events.title: General election results
events.description: India VIX climbed steadily through the weeks before the results and jumped again on result day, then fell back quickly once the outcome was clear. Chapter 3 examines this period in detail.

events.title: Cheap insurance
events.description: In quiet markets, India VIX has spent long periods at roughly 10 to 14, when three months of out-of-the-money cover costs well under 1% of a portfolio.

children.text: Buying in the Panic: What Late Hedgers Pay

Suppose the Nifty has already fallen 16% to 21,000 and IV has jumped to 40%. An investor now wants the same kind of hedge as before: a three-month put about 4% below the market, the 20,150 strike. The model price is about ₹1,105, or 5.26% of the index level. In a calm market with IV at 15%, the same strike at the same Nifty level would cost about ₹195, or 0.93%. The late hedger pays roughly 5.7 times as much, and is insuring a portfolio that has already absorbed a 16% loss.

body.title: When is cover most expensive?
body.question: All four cases involve buying a three-month Nifty put about 4% below the current Nifty level. In which case will the premium, as a percentage of the Nifty, be highest?
options: India VIX at 11, two weeks after a quiet quarterly results season
India VIX at 15, one month before the Union Budget
India VIX at 34, the day after a sharp 5% one-day fall in the Nifty
India VIX at 18, during a steady rally to new highs
body.explanation: With strike distance and term the same in percentage terms, the premium as a percentage of the index is driven mainly by implied volatility. India VIX at 34 signals very high IV, so that put costs by far the most, often several times the calm-market price.

body.title: Where India VIX comes from
body.textWithBlank: India VIX is calculated by NSE from the prices of Nifty ___.
body.explanation: India VIX backs out the market's expected volatility from near-month and next-month Nifty option prices. That is why it moves together with the cost of protection.

body.title: The hidden bonus: why an existing hedge gains when fear rises

markDefs.definition: How much an option's price changes for a one percentage point change in implied volatility. Long puts gain value when implied volatility rises.

children.text: If you already hold a put when fear arrives, rising IV works for you. Your put gains from the market falling and again from IV rising. That second effect is called
. Take Ananya's hedge from Chapter 1: one lot of the three-month 24,000 put bought at ₹250 in a calm market. One month later, the Nifty has dropped to 23,000.

content.caption: Ananya's put one month in, Nifty at 23,000, two months left (illustrative model prices)

children.text: The jump in IV adds ₹22,815 to her hedge. This is one more reason to buy protection before fear rises: the calm-market buyer pays low IV and then benefits when it rises, while the panic buyer pays high IV and often loses value as it falls back.

body.text: A low India VIX is not a signal that a crash is coming, and a high one is not a signal that the bottom is in. VIX tells you the price of protection, not the direction of the market. The discipline is to decide whether you need a hedge based on your goals and tolerable drawdown, then use VIX to judge whether now is a cheap or expensive time to buy it.

body.title: Karthik waits for the storm
body.scenario: Karthik, 53, a chartered engineer in Coimbatore, has ₹50 lakh in equity funds and plans to use ₹20 lakh for his son's overseas master's degree in nine months. Six months ago, with India VIX at 12, his adviser suggested a put hedge on part of the portfolio. Karthik declined: "The market is calm, I'll hedge when it starts looking risky." Today the Nifty is 12% below its peak, India VIX is at 32, and the news is full of warnings. He now wants to buy puts on his entire ₹50 lakh.
body.prompt: What has changed about the cost and usefulness of a hedge since six months ago, and what would you advise Karthik to do now?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cost: with VIX at 32 against 12 before, the same percentage-distance put now costs several times more. Hedging all ₹50 lakh for three months could cost 3% to 4% of the portfolio or more.
2. Usefulness: his portfolio has already absorbed roughly a 12% fall. A new put 4% below today's level protects only from here, so his worst case from the peak is now around 16% plus a large premium, not the roughly 5% he could have locked in earlier.
3. Sizing: his real need is ₹20 lakh in nine months, not the whole ₹50 lakh. Insuring everything at peak prices compounds the mistake.
4. Better options now: move part of the ₹20 lakh into debt in stages, which costs no premium; if he still wants a hedge, cover only the portion tied to the goal, use a lower strike or a collar to reduce the cost, and accept that some protection is now simply expensive.
5. For next time: write a hedging plan when markets are calm, based on goals and tolerable drawdown, so the decision is not made in fear.
The lesson: waiting for a hedge to feel necessary almost guarantees paying the most for the least protection.

body.title: Check the price of fear before you hedge
steps: Look up today's India VIX on the NSE website and convert it to an expected one-month move.
Compare today's level with its range over the past year to see whether protection is currently cheap or expensive.
Note the implied volatility shown for your chosen strike on the NSE option chain.
Calculate the premium as a percentage of the amount you are covering, for the full term.
If VIX is high, price at least one cheaper alternative: a lower strike, a partial hedge, or moving part of the money to debt.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Premiums are illustrative estimates from a standard pricing model at flat implied volatility, and real market prices will differ. Historical India VIX levels are approximate. The VIX bands are a rough guide, not trading signals. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before using options.
